claims.text: Controlled low-temperature annealing will relieve residual internal strain in as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Controlled low-temperature annealing will enhance short-range chemical order in as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Low-temperature annealing may produce a moderate density of nanoscale features.
Annealing-induced strain relief and ordering will principally modify grain-boundary regions.
Annealing-induced homogenization will make the local magnetostructural transition more uniform.
Grain boundaries and localized chemical-disorder or strain regions mediate nucleation and growth of the ferromagnetic phase.
Microstructural homogenization will reduce the nucleation energy barriers of the ferromagnetic phase during cycling.
Annealing will reduce the dispersion of local transition temperatures.
Strain relief and enhanced short-range order will lower barriers for magnetic-domain reorientation during the phase transition.
Lower kinetic barriers will make the magnetocaloric change less abrupt and more distributed in temperature.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower thermal hysteresis than the as-deposited control under approximately 0.5–1 T cycling.
Annealed samples will exhibit a broader and smoother magnetic-entropy-change profile than the as-deposited control.
A smoother magnetocaloric response will enhance effective heat exchange.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy is an ordered, single-phase hexagonal material.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits significant thermal hysteresis.
The as-deposited alloy has substantial heterogeneity in local strain and chemical order.
Local strain and chemical-order heterogeneity cause large hysteretic losses during low-field cooling cycles.
Larger grain sizes limit heat exchange in the as-deposited material.
The predictions apply only while annealing avoids secondary phases, excessive coarsening, and loss of mechanical stability.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says annealing reduces the dispersion of local transition temperatures, but the predicted response is broader and more distributed in temperature. The hypothesis does not explain how a narrower local-transition distribution produces this broadening.
